Why Does My Implant Crown Feel Slightly Different After Several Years?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

It is not uncommon for patients to notice that their implant crown feels slightly different after several years — perhaps a subtle change in the way it bites, a minor shift in sensation, or simply a feeling that is hard to put into words. Many people turn to the internet for reassurance, unsure whether this is a normal sign of aging in the restoration or something that warrants a closer look.

Dental implant crowns are designed to be long-lasting and highly functional, but like all dental restorations, they exist within a dynamic oral environment that changes over time. The surrounding gum tissue, adjacent natural teeth, and even the position of your jaw can evolve across the years.

This article aims to explain the most common reasons why an implant crown may feel different after several years, what changes are considered normal, and which situations may benefit from a professional dental assessment. Understanding these factors can help you feel more informed and confident about your dental health.

An implant crown feeling slightly different after several years is relatively common and may result from changes in bite alignment, natural wear of the crown material, minor shifts in surrounding gum tissue, or slight loosening of the abutment screw. While some changes are normal, a dental examination can help determine whether any adjustment or intervention is appropriate.

What Is an Implant Crown and How Does It Work?

A dental implant crown is the visible, tooth-like restoration that sits on top of the titanium implant fixture embedded in the jawbone. It is typically connected via a small component called an abutment, which acts as a connector between the implant body and the crown itself.

Unlike natural teeth, implant crowns do not have a periodontal ligament — the network of fibres that connects natural tooth roots to the surrounding bone and provides sensory feedback. This means the way you perceive biting force and sensation through an implant crown is inherently different from a natural tooth, and this difference may become more noticeable over time, particularly as the surrounding natural teeth experience their own age-related changes.

The crown material — whether porcelain, zirconia, or a composite — is highly durable, but it is not impervious to gradual wear or minor changes over years of normal function. Understanding the nature of these restorations helps contextualise why subtle changes in feel can occur and why monitoring them professionally is a sensible approach.

Common Reasons an Implant Crown May Feel Different Over Time

There are several well-recognised reasons why an implant crown might feel subtly different after several years of use. These range from entirely normal wear-related changes to situations that may warrant clinical review.

Natural wear of crown material: Over time, the biting surface of an implant crown can undergo gradual wear, especially in patients who grind or clench their teeth. This may alter the feel of the bite slightly.

Changes in adjacent natural teeth: Natural teeth can shift, wear down, or be restored, all of which may subtly change the relationship between the implant crown and surrounding teeth.

Gum tissue changes: The soft tissue around the implant may remodel gently over years, affecting the way the crown sits at the gum margin and how it feels when touched.

Bite changes: Your overall bite pattern — known as occlusion — can change due to factors such as tooth movement, restoration of other teeth, or changes in the jaw joint.

Abutment screw dynamics: In some cases, the small internal screw holding the crown to the implant can loosen marginally over time, creating a subtle change in the feel of the crown during biting. This is often discussed clinically as a loose implant screw.

If you have noticed any of these changes, scheduling a review with your dental professional is a reasonable and sensible step.

The Clinical Science Behind How Implant Crowns Interact With the Jaw

To understand why implant crowns can feel different over time, it helps to consider some of the underlying dental science — explained in straightforward terms.

Natural teeth are suspended in the jaw by the periodontal ligament, a dense network of fibres that acts almost like a subtle shock absorber. This ligament also provides proprioception — essentially, the sensory awareness of how hard you are biting and where your teeth are meeting. When a tooth is replaced with a dental implant, this ligament is absent. The implant integrates directly with the bone in a process called osseointegration, which is what makes implants stable and long-lasting.

However, because there is no periodontal ligament, the brain receives different sensory feedback from an implant crown compared to a natural tooth. Over time, your natural teeth may migrate or wear slightly, while the implant crown remains fixed. This mismatch between the static implant crown and the evolving natural dentition can contribute to subtle changes in how the crown feels during biting, chewing, or even at rest.

Additionally, the surrounding bone itself can undergo minor remodelling over many years, which may subtly influence the gum profile around the implant. This is a natural biological process, not necessarily a sign that anything is wrong — though it is worth monitoring.

To learn more about how dental implants integrate with the jaw and what to expect long-term, explore our single tooth implant treatment information.

Signs That Might Benefit From a Professional Dental Review

While many subtle changes in how an implant crown feels are benign, there are certain symptoms that make a professional dental assessment a sensible course of action. It is important to approach these calmly — experiencing any of the following does not automatically indicate a serious problem, but a clinical examination can provide clarity.

You may wish to arrange a dental review if you notice:

  • A change in how the crown meets the opposing teeth during biting or chewing
  • Any sensation of movement or looseness in the crown
  • Tenderness or mild discomfort in the gum tissue around the implant
  • Visible changes in the gum margin, such as recession revealing the edge of the crown
  • Difficulty chewing on the side where the implant is located
  • A feeling that the crown is sitting higher or lower than before
  • Any persistent sensitivity in the surrounding area

None of these symptoms should be a cause for alarm, but they do benefit from professional assessment. Early review often means straightforward management — for example, a simple bite adjustment or retightening of an abutment screw — rather than more complex intervention later.

If you have concerns about your implant, arranging a dental implant review with a qualified dental professional is a sensible first step.

How Bite Changes Can Affect the Feel of an Implant Crown

The way your upper and lower teeth meet — your occlusion — is not static. Over the course of several years, a range of factors can cause the bite to shift, and these changes may be particularly noticeable in relation to an implant crown.

Natural teeth have a small degree of movement within the periodontal ligament, allowing them to adapt gradually to bite forces and minor positional changes. An implant crown, firmly anchored in bone, cannot move in the same way. As a result, if the surrounding natural teeth shift — even by a fraction of a millimetre — the implant crown may begin to feel like it is in a slightly different position relative to the bite. If this topic sounds familiar, you may also find this article on teeth shifting around an existing implant helpful.

Similarly, if other teeth have been restored, crowned, or extracted since the implant was placed, these changes alter the overall bite pattern. Jaw joint changes, which can occur with age or as a result of habits such as teeth grinding, may also influence the feel of the bite.

In many cases, a straightforward bite adjustment — a procedure known as occlusal equilibration — carried out during a routine dental review can resolve the sensation effectively. This involves the dentist carefully assessing where the teeth meet and making minor, precise adjustments to the crown surface. It is a conservative and common procedure.

The Role of Teeth Grinding and Clenching (Bruxism)

Bruxism — the habit of grinding or clenching the teeth, often during sleep — is a significant factor in how dental restorations perform and feel over time. Many people are unaware they grind their teeth until a dentist identifies signs of wear.

For patients with implant crowns, bruxism can accelerate wear of the crown surface, potentially alter the bite, and place additional stress on the implant and abutment. Over several years, this may contribute to the sensation that the crown feels different or that the bite has changed.

If bruxism is identified, a custom-made occlusal splint (sometimes called a night guard) is often recommended. This is a removable appliance worn during sleep that helps to protect both natural teeth and implant restorations from the effects of grinding forces. It does not cure bruxism, but it serves as an effective protective measure.

Discussing your habits with your dentist — including any jaw soreness in the morning, headaches, or tooth sensitivity — can help identify whether bruxism may be contributing to any changes you are experiencing with your implant crown.

Maintenance and Prevention: Caring for Your Implant Crown Long-Term

Good maintenance is fundamental to the long-term performance and comfort of a dental implant crown. While implant crowns cannot develop decay in the way natural teeth can, the surrounding tissues and the implant components require consistent care.

Practical steps to support long-term implant health:

  • Brush twice daily using a soft-bristled toothbrush, ensuring you clean gently around the base of the implant crown where it meets the gum.
  • Use interdental cleaning aids such as floss, interdental brushes, or a water flosser to clean between the implant crown and adjacent teeth.
  • Attend routine dental and hygiene appointments so that any changes in the crown, bite, or surrounding tissues can be identified and addressed promptly.
  • Inform your dentist of any changes in how the crown feels, even if subtle. Changes noted early are generally easier to manage.
  • Wear a night guard if recommended, particularly if you are aware of or have been advised about teeth grinding or clenching.
  • Avoid very hard foods that place excessive force on any dental restoration, including implant crowns.
  • Do not use your teeth as tools — opening packaging or biting fingernails can place unexpected stress on restorations.

For comprehensive guidance on looking after your implant long-term, your dental hygienist is an excellent resource and can tailor advice to your individual situation. Learn more about professional implant maintenance support and how regular visits can contribute to implant longevity.

Key Points to Remember

  • It is relatively common for an implant crown to feel subtly different after several years of use.
  • Changes may be due to natural wear of the crown material, bite changes, gum tissue remodelling, or minor loosening of the abutment screw.
  • Because implant crowns do not have a periodontal ligament, they interact with the bite differently to natural teeth, and this difference may become more noticeable over time.
  • Many changes are manageable with straightforward dental review and conservative adjustments.
  • Symptoms such as looseness, persistent discomfort, or visible gum changes around the implant are worth having assessed professionally.
  • Consistent home care and regular dental appointments are the foundation of long-term implant crown health.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a dental implant crown to feel different after a few years?

Yes, it is not unusual for patients to notice subtle changes in how an implant crown feels after several years. Factors such as natural wear of the crown surface, changes in surrounding teeth, bite evolution, and gum tissue remodelling can all contribute. Because implant crowns are fixed in bone without a periodontal ligament, they do not adapt to bite changes in the way natural teeth do. If the change is notable or accompanied by other symptoms, a dental review is advisable.

Could my implant crown be loose?

It is possible for the abutment screw — which connects the crown to the implant body — to loosen over time. This may produce a sensation of slight movement or instability in the crown. This is generally a straightforward matter for a dental professional to address. It is important not to ignore this sensation, as a loose crown left unmanaged may put uneven stress on the implant. A routine appointment to assess and, if needed, retighten the screw is the appropriate course of action.

Can the gum around an implant crown change over time?

Yes, the gum tissue surrounding a dental implant can undergo gradual changes over the years. Minor recession or remodelling of the soft tissue is a recognised occurrence and may cause the crown to appear to sit slightly differently. In some cases, the edge of the crown or the abutment beneath may become marginally visible. Regular professional monitoring allows any changes to be tracked and assessed within the context of your overall implant health.

Does teeth grinding affect an implant crown differently to a natural tooth?

Yes, bruxism (teeth grinding and clenching) can affect implant crowns differently to natural teeth. Natural teeth have some degree of flexibility due to the periodontal ligament, whereas implant crowns are rigidly anchored. This means grinding forces are transmitted differently, and there is a potential for accelerated wear on the crown surface. If you grind your teeth, your dentist may recommend a protective night guard to preserve both your implant restoration and natural teeth.

How often should I have my dental implant reviewed?

Most dental professionals recommend a clinical review of your dental implant at least once a year, typically as part of your routine dental examination. Some patients may benefit from more frequent monitoring, particularly if there are concerns about gum health, bite changes, or implant stability. Your dentist and hygienist are best placed to recommend a review schedule suited to your individual circumstances and oral health needs.

When should I contact my dentist about a change in my implant crown?

You should contact your dentist if you notice any of the following: a sensation of movement or looseness in the crown, persistent discomfort or tenderness around the implant, a notable change in how the crown feels during biting or chewing, visible changes in the surrounding gum tissue, or any swelling or unusual appearance in the area. These symptoms do not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but they benefit from timely professional assessment to determine the appropriate course of action.

Conclusion

If your implant crown feels slightly different after several years, you are not alone in noticing this. The oral environment changes naturally over time, and a fixed implant crown exists within a dynamic system of natural teeth, gum tissue, and bone that continues to evolve. In many cases, the changes you perceive are the result of normal processes such as crown wear, bite evolution, or minor gum tissue remodelling — all of which can be assessed and managed effectively with professional guidance.

What matters most is that you do not dismiss subtle changes or feel uncertain about whether to seek advice. Early professional review is generally straightforward and can provide reassurance or identify a minor adjustment that restores your comfort and confidence in your restoration.

Regular dental examinations and professional hygiene visits remain among the most effective ways to monitor the long-term health and performance of your dental implant, alongside a consistent home care routine.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
